test_texts:
PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 35394/97) against [LOCATION] [LOCATION] and [LOCATION] lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), a [LOCATION] national, on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the Commission (First Chamber) decided to give notice of the application to the United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) and invited them to submit observations on its admissibility and merits.

The Government submitted their observations on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant replied on [DATE_TIME], after an extension of the time-limit fixed for that purpose. On [DATE_TIME] the Government made comments on the applicant's observations in reply.

Following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on [DATE_TIME], and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 2 thereof, the case was examined by the Court.

In accordance with Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court, the President of the Court, Mr [PERSON], assigned the case to the Third Section.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to a hearing on the merits.

On [DATE_TIME] the President granted leave to the non-governmental organisations Justice and Liberty to submit joint written comments in connection with the case (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 61 § 3).

The hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr [PERSON], Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Lord [PERSON] of Mostyn QC, Attorney-General, Mr [PERSON], Counsel, [PERSON], [PERSON], Advisers; (b) for the applicant Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Counsel, Mr [PERSON], of the Sheffield Bar, Solicitor. The Court heard addresses by Mr [PERSON] and Lord [PERSON].

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant arrived at [LOCATION] on a flight from [LOCATION]. On the same flight was his cousin, [PERSON] Both men were stopped and searched by customs officials. [PERSON] was found to be in possession of heroin with a street value of almost 100,000 pounds sterling. He was interviewed and then arrested and charged. No drugs were found on the applicant. He too was interviewed, but made no admissions. He was released without charge. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant visited a friend, [PERSON], in [LOCATION]. [PERSON] was under investigation for dealing in heroin. On [DATE_TIME] the installation of a listening device on B.'s premises had been authorised by the Chief Constable of [LOCATION] on the grounds that the conventional methods of surveillance were unlikely to provide proof that he was dealing in drugs. It was not expected or foreseen that the applicant would visit the premises. Neither B. nor the applicant was aware of the aural surveillance equipment which had been installed by the police.

By means of that device the police obtained a tape recording of a conversation, in the course of which the applicant admitted that he had been a party to the importation of drugs by N. on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant was arrested on [DATE_TIME]. Again he made no admissions when interviewed, but subsequently he and [PERSON] were jointly charged with offences under the Customs and Excise Management Act 1979 and the Misuse of Drugs Act [DATE_TIME] and committed for trial.

The trial took place in [DATE_TIME]. The applicant pleaded “not guilty”. The applicant admitted that he had been present at the [LOCATION] address and that his voice was one of those recorded on the tape. It was admitted on behalf of the Crown that the attachment of the listening device had involved a civil trespass and had occasioned some damage to the property. Thereupon, the trial judge conducted a hearing on the voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of the jury) as to the admissibility in evidence of the conversation recorded on the tape. The Crown accepted that without it there was no case against the applicant.

The trial judge ruled that the evidence was admissible. Following an amendment to the indictment, the applicant was re-arraigned and pleaded guilty to being knowingly concerned in the fraudulent evasion of the prohibition on the importation of heroin. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was sentenced to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment.

The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal on the ground that the evidence ought to have been held to be inadmissible. On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against conviction but also certified, as a point of law of general public importance, the question whether evidence of tape-recorded conversations, obtained by a listening device attached by the police to a private house without the knowledge of the owners or occupiers, was admissible in a criminal trial against the defendant.

On [DATE_TIME] the Appeal Committee of the House of Lords granted the applicant leave to appeal from the decision of the Court of Appeal dismissing his appeal against conviction. On [DATE_TIME] the House of Lords dismissed the applicant's appeal. The House of Lords noted that the question before it gave rise to two separate issues, the first being whether evidence of the taped conversations was admissible at all and the second whether, if admissible, it should nonetheless have been excluded by the trial judge in the exercise of his discretion at common law or under the powers conferred by section 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act [DATE_TIME] (“PACE”). As to the former issue, the House of Lords held that there was no right to privacy in English law and that, even if there were such a right, the common-law rule that relevant evidence which was obtained improperly or even unlawfully remained admissible applied to evidence obtained by the use of surveillance devices which invaded a person's privacy. As to the latter issue, it was held that the fact that evidence had been obtained in circumstances which amounted to a breach of the provisions of Article 8 of the Convention was relevant to, but not determinative of, the judge's discretion to admit or exclude such evidence under section 78 of PACE. The judge's discretion had to be exercised according to whether the admission of the evidence would render the trial unfair, and the use at a criminal trial of material obtained in breach of the right to privacy enshrined in Article 8 did not mean that the trial would be unfair. On the facts, the trial judge had been entitled to hold that the circumstances in which the relevant evidence was obtained, even if they constituted a breach of Article 8, were not such as to require the exclusion of the evidence. Lord [PERSON], giving the opinion of the majority of the House, added: “The sole cause of this case coming to your Lordship's House is the lack of a statutory system regulating the use of surveillance devices by the police. The absence of such a system seems astonishing, the more so in view of the statutory framework which has governed the use of such devices by the Security Service since [DATE_TIME], and the interception of communications by the police as well as by other agencies since [DATE_TIME]. I would refrain from other comment because counsel for the respondent was able to inform us, on instructions, that the government proposes to introduce legislation covering the matter in the next session of Parliament.”

The applicant was discharged from prison on [DATE_TIME]. His release was on licence until [DATE_TIME].

for the Commission Sir [PERSON], Delegate;

for the applicants Mr. [PERSON], [PERSON], Mr. [PERSON], Barrister-at-Law, Counsel. The Court heard addresses by Mr. [PERSON] for the Government, by Sir [PERSON] for the Commission and by Mr. [PERSON] for the applicants, as well as their replies to its questions. [DATE_TIME], the Government lodged at the registry various documents the production of which the Registrar had previously, on [DATE_TIME], requested on the instructions of the President of the Chamber.

Following deliberations held on [DATE_TIME], the Chamber, by unanimous decision, relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the plenary Court (Rule 50). Having taken note of the agreement of the Agent of the Government and the concurring opinion of the Delegate of the Commission and of the applicants, the Court decided on [DATE_TIME], that the consideration of the case should continue without resumption of the oral proceedings (Rule 26).

AS TO THE FACTS

I. PARTICULAR CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

[PERSON] and [PERSON]

The applicants, [PERSON] and [PERSON], are [NRP] citizens born in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] respectively. In [DATE_TIME], the first applicant was sentenced in [LOCATION] to life imprisonment for murder. He received a number of subsequent prison sentences in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] for prison breaking, attempted murder of a prison officer and assault on prison staff. The second applicant is the first applicant’s wife and a doctor by profession.

In [DATE_TIME], Mr. [PERSON] was removed from Peterhead Prison to a Special Unit in [LOCATION]. This Unit had been set up on an experimental basis to treat selected long-term prisoners and prisoners with violent propensities (see paragraph 32 below). The Unit had a maximum of eight prisoners and was characterised by a more liberal regime. Mr. [PERSON] played a prominent role in facilitating the success of the Special Unit. In particular, he discovered that he had special abilities in working with people and in sculpture, writing and other areas of artistic activity. While in the Special Unit, Mr. [PERSON] was allowed, amongst other things, to write and receive uncensored mail, to have [DATE_TIME] access to visitors and to use a telephone. He was thereby able to meet his wife, talk to her on the telephone and correspond with her without being subject to the normal restrictions. He also had the opportunity to go out of the prison without escort.

In [DATE_TIME], Mr. [PERSON] was advised by the Parole Board that he was to be released on licence in [DATE_TIME] and that he was to be transferred to [LOCATION], [LOCATION], to undergo a pre-release programme. He was informed that he would serve his time there on the same terms and conditions as other prisoners. It was considered that, although the regime there was on traditional lines, [LOCATION] would be more beneficial to Mr. [PERSON] during the period leading to his eventual release than other alternatives, for example Penninghame Open Prison (see paragraph 31 below). The factors governing the choice included the desirability of his occupying a single cell rather than being in a dormitory; the availability of suitable [DATE_TIME]-time work for him and of facilities for continuing his studies and his artistic work; and access to suitable educational and vocational opportunities for his pre-release training. Mr. [PERSON] himself had in fact stated in written submissions in [DATE_TIME] that, if he could not remain at [PERSON] for his pre-release programme, he would prefer training from [LOCATION] rather than [LOCATION]. In [DATE_TIME], he was transferred to a Training for Freedom Hostel within the prison (see paragraph 33 below). He was released on [DATE_TIME]. As from [DATE_TIME] until his release, he was in the lowest security category (Category D).

The applicants’ complaints to the Commission in so far as relevant to the present proceedings all related to the period [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] when Mr. [PERSON] was subject to the ordinary prison regime at [LOCATION]. The facts surrounding those grievances are briefly set out in the following paragraphs.

During the relevant period the normal rules regarding the sending and payment of correspondence were applied to Mr. [PERSON] (see paragraphs 22 and 23 below). The postage of only one three-page letter [DATE_TIME] was paid for out of public funds. He was able to pay for other letters out of his prison earnings of £1.60 per week but not out of his general financial resources. In a letter of [DATE_TIME] from his solicitors to the Secretary of State for [LOCATION], a complaint was made that because he found it necessary to spend 80 pence per week out of his earnings to supplement his (mainly) vegetarian diet by buying oatmeal cakes as the prison service provided only white bread, the number of letters he was able to send was restricted. A full vegetarian diet was available at [LOCATION] and no complaint was made by Mr. [PERSON] to the Governor or to the Secretary of State as to its adequacy.

Mr. [PERSON]’s incoming and outgoing mail was controlled by the prison authorities in accordance with the normal practice followed at the prison (see paragraph 24 below). The applicants also asserted before the Commission that on occasions the prison censorship officer read out aloud in front of other inmates letters from Mrs. [PERSON], laughing or making comments about their contents. However, Mr. [PERSON] did not make any complaint to the Governor of the Prison or the Secretary of State regarding the manner in which his mail was read, in particular about its being read aloud, although the fact of his mail being screened was the subject of complaint in his solicitors’ letter of [DATE_TIME].

In [DATE_TIME], a letter to a friend of his, Mr. [PERSON], was stopped by the Prison Governor on the ground that Mr. [PERSON] was a “media personality“. Mr. [PERSON] petitioned the Secretary of State regarding this matter, but his petition was rejected on the basis that there was a general prohibition of the passing on by a prisoner of material intended for publication or for use on wireless or television (see paragraph 25 below). The Government have subsequently acknowledged that in fact this rule was applied in error, since, although the letter in question was addressed to a person connected with the public media, it was a personal one which Mr. [PERSON] should have been allowed to send.

Mr. [PERSON] was entitled to receive visits in accordance with the normal rules applied in [LOCATION] (see paragraph 26 below). Consequently, as pointed out in his solicitors’ letter of [DATE_TIME], he was permitted [DATE_TIME]’s visiting time [DATE_TIME] under close supervision in a crowded visiting hall. He used this time to meet his wife, with the result that he was not able to see the other members of his family. He was able to benefit from the special escorted leave scheme and visited his home on two occasions, albeit under the constant supervision of an officer in accordance with the scheme (see paragraph 28 below). As from [DATE_TIME], he was given a special licence to do unescorted community work outside the prison, initially for [DATE_TIME] and subsequently for [DATE_TIME] a week.

The solicitors for Mr. and Mrs. [PERSON] also raised with the Secretary of State a general objection that Mr. [PERSON]’s treatment at [LOCATION] was markedly less favourable than his treatment at Barlinnie Special Unit and also in comparison with other Category D prisoners elsewhere under the penal system. By reply dated [DATE_TIME], the Secretary of State rejected this and the other complaints made in the solicitors’ letter of [DATE_TIME]. Mr. [PERSON] also complained through his Member of Parliament to the Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration (the Ombudsman - see paragraph 39 below) about various aspects of his treatment at [LOCATION]. In a letter of [DATE_TIME], the Ombudsman stated that he could not uphold Mr. [PERSON]’s complaints. He stated, inter alia: “From the details that Mr. [PERSON] has given, his correspondence, special escorted leave, and visits appear to have been dealt with correctly in accordance with current rules, however dissatisfied he may be with those rules. I think it is fair to say that much of Mr. [PERSON]’s complaint reflects his disagreement with those rules and with their application to him at this stage of his sentence. The rules are of course a matter for Parliament and in the absence of evidence of maladministration I am precluded by the Parliamentary Commissioner Act from questioning the Department’s discretion in applying them.“

[PERSON] and [PERSON]

The applicants, [PERSON] and [PERSON], are [NRP] citizens born in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] respectively. [PERSON] was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder in [DATE_TIME]. He served his sentence in [PERSON] and Perth Prisons until [DATE_TIME]. From [DATE_TIME] onwards, he was detained as a Category D prisoner (that is, the lowest security category) at [LOCATION]. He was moved to the Training for Freedom Hostel within the prison (see paragraph 33 below) on [DATE_TIME] and was released on licence on [DATE_TIME]. He had requested to serve the latter part of his sentence in [LOCATION] rather than, for example, in Penninghame Open Prison (see paragraph 31 below) because he wanted, prior to his release, to have the benefit of further education courses which were not available from [LOCATION]. [PERSON] is the first-named applicant’s father and lives at [LOCATION], some sixty miles from [LOCATION]. At the relevant time he was seriously ill - having been in bad health for some years - and unable to walk or travel.

During his period in [LOCATION], [PERSON] enjoyed the normal entitlement to visits applicable at the prison. He petitioned the Secretary of State for [LOCATION] on [DATE_TIME] requesting a home visit to his father. The petition indicated that his father had been “ill for a considerable period“, but not that he was dangerously ill, which would have made him eligible for compassionate leave (see paragraph 27 below). His request was therefore refused on [DATE_TIME]. The decision recommended him to make the effort to get a member of staff to take him out of prison under the special escorted leave scheme (see paragraph 28 below). It appears, however, that he experienced difficulty in finding a prison officer to accompany him on special escorted leave. Although [PERSON] was not able to visit his father during the relevant period, he was permitted to attend, without an escort, a college to follow an educational course [DATE_TIME] a week and also a centre where he was doing community work. He had previously been granted a home visit in [DATE_TIME] and prior to the commencement of the Training for Freedom programme he spent [DATE_TIME] on home leave in [DATE_TIME]. In a letter dated [DATE_TIME] in reply to a letter of [DATE_TIME] from Mr. [PERSON]’s Member of Parliament, the Under Secretary of State at the Scottish Office explained the reasons for the refusal of compassionate leave: “... Each application is considered on its merits and on the basis of medical and social work reports. Mr. [PERSON]’s application for a special visit was considered in the usual way but it was decided that it did not meet the required conditions. Mr. [PERSON] was advised that if his father’s condition deteriorated he should make a further request. It is necessary, to prevent abuse of the arrangements, to maintain a strict and entirely consistent approach to applications for compassionate visits from all prisoners and the fact that a prisoner is being released for educational or other purposes does not affect consideration of the merits of his application or remove the need for the normal criteria to be met. ... Mr. [PERSON] is expected to transfer to the formal Training for Freedom (TFF) in [DATE_TIME]. Prior to that he will have a [DATE_TIME] home leave and while on TFF he will have [DATE_TIME] which he may spend at home. I feel that it would be quite wrong, before that stage is reached, to make a special exception in Mr. [PERSON]’s case and circumvent the rules in relation to either a compassionate visit or a special escorted leave.“

On [DATE_TIME], the solicitors acting for [PERSON] wrote to the Secretary of State complaining about

the alleged stopping by the prison authorities of a number of letters addressed to themselves, his Member of Parliament, his former counsel and his family;

his limited prison visiting entitlement, which, as regards maintenance of family contacts, was said to discriminate against him in comparison with other prisoners who were in Category D but detained in open conditions; and

the refusal to grant compassionate leave. The reply of [DATE_TIME] sent on behalf of the Secretary of State rejected all the various complaints raised. In particular, it was pointed out that all his mail had been posted.

name: Gustav Adolf
train_texts: The [PERSON] case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and the Government of the Republic of Austria. The case originated in an application against this State lodged with the Commission on [DATE_TIME] under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention by an [NRP] citizen. Their purpose is to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 par. 1, 2 and 3 (d) ( art. 6-1, 6-2, 4-3-d) The Government's application asks the Court in particular to find that there has been no such breach in this case. The oral hearings took place in public at [LOCATION], [ LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. Immediately before their opening, the Court had held a preparatory meeting at which it had authorised the person assisting the Delegate of the Commission to address the Court in German (Rule 27 par. 3). There appeared before the Court: Mr. [PERSON], Ambassador, Ministry or Foreign Affairs, Agent, Advocate-General, Ministry of Justice, Oberrat, Federal Chancellery, Constitutional Department, Advisers; and the applicant's lawyer before the Commission. The Court heard addresses and replies to questions put by the Court. Those appearing before the court filed several documents during the hearings. The applicant, an [NRP] citizen born in [DATE_TIME], lives in [LOCATION] where he practises the profession of accountant and financial consultant ([PERSON). He denied the facts alleged against him and denounced the complaint as being knowingly false. He said that the object alleged to have caused the injury was, in fact, an envelope containing a single key, which had slipped out of his hand and touched her arm. The police accepted the note, but did not question Mrs. [PERSON] or the employees. The public prosecutor's office, to which the file had been returned, asked the Innsbruck District Court to procure a medical report. The Court registered the case on [DATE_TIME]; under the heading “punishable act’ it specified “section 83 of the Penal Code’ The District Court assessed the costs of that opinion. Mr. [PERSON] denied that he had injured Mrs. ERSON, whether by throwing a bunch of keys or otherwise, and contested the doctor's findings. He claimed in particular that the latter had based his opinion on information that was contradicted by the material in the case-file (aktenwidrig). He called on the District Court either to acquit him after trial or to terminate the proceedings pursuant to section 90 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. District Court of Innsbruck, Section 9, [DATE_TIME].“The applicant challenged this decision before the Regional Court (Landesgericht) of [LOCATION] which declared the appeal inadmissible on the ground that section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure limited the right of appeal to the prosecutor’s office.” “The defendant (Beschuldigter) threw an envelope containing a key in the direction of Mrs. [PERSON] who however managed to avoid the missile. The key first struck the back of the right hand, causing a superficial abrasion, and then bounced against the left side of the above-named person's chest. No injury could be established on the chest. The injury found (festgestellte) is insignificant. The fault (Verschulden) of the accused may be described as insignificant (geringfügig), and his character gives cause to expect that he will conduct himself properly in future.“ Generalprokurator (the public prosecutor attached to the Supreme Court) filed an application for annulment of the decision dated [DATE_TIME] in the interests of the proper application of the law. He drew a distinction between the termination of. proceedings by virtue of section 451 par. 2 and their termination by virtue. of section 90 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In both cases, he said, the decisions would be taken without the formal hearing of evidence, something which, as followed in any event from Article 6 par. 6-1, should in principle precede any finding of guilt (Schulderkenntnis) The Generalprokurator moved the Supreme Court to hold that the Innsbruck District Court's decision dated [DATE_TIME] was, as regards its reasoning, contrary to the law. Mr. [PERSON] criticised the District Court for having failed to satisfy essential elements of violation of the law inherent in the impugned decision. He disputed the interpretation of section 42 of the Penal Code which required the court to make a positive finding of an act fulfilling the description of a criminal offence. He relied on section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which places the judge under a duty to satisfy himself, before bringing the proceedings to a close, that the conditions stipulated under section 42 are met. The suspect accused the Generalprokurator of breaching Article 6 par. 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention. He called on the Supreme Court to find infringements of the law. The Supreme Court rejected the application for annulment on [DATE_TIME]. In the opinion, the application of section 42 par.1 of the Penal Code did not place the suspect in a worse position than where the case is closed for some other reason. The person concerned thus has no right to have doubtful issues in the case clarified. Section 42 simply requires the existence of a suspicion. The decision contains - if only because of its very nature - a negative ruling on the merits of the case. It would certainly have been preferable had the Innsbruck District Court stated this explicitly and without ambiguity in the decision being challenged. But the more or less apposite choice of wording in the reasoning could not deprive the reasoning of the specific significance it had as a result of the nature of the decision given. Since legal proof of the suspect's guilt is not the object pursued under section 42 of the Penal Code, no question arises as to the extent to which a decision given in pursuance of this provision has or has not been preceded by proceedings complying with the requirements of Article 6 par. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. The applicant himself had to pay his lawyer's fees and his own expenses. The public prosecutor has a duty to cause the competent court to take the necessary measures of investigation and punishment (section 34 par. 1) If sufficient grounds for prosecuting the individual in question are lacking, the public prosecutor shall take no further action on the complaint and shall transmit the file to the investigating judge. The judge must then terminate the preliminary enquiries. In district court proceedings there is no formal process of investigation. All that is required is a written or oral application from the district prosecutor seeking the imposition of a penalty on the person concerned. In cases before a district court, the decision terminating proceedings is governed by section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Section 42 was introduced into the new Austrian Penal Code which entered into force on [DATE_TIME], and is aimed at avoiding criminal trials in trivial cases. The Supreme Court and the great majority of legal commentators regard it as a clause which is not concerned with mere procedure but which provides a substantive ground for exonerating the accused. A decision taken by a court in pursuance of section 42 to terminate proceedings is not entered in the criminal record of the person concerned. The file relating to a case closed in this manner may be used in other legal (and disciplinary) proceedings, as may, in principle, the case-file in any legal action whatever its outcome. The Commission accepted the application on [DATE_TIME]. The Government requested the Court ‘to hold that in the present case the provisions of paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 (d) of Article 6 were not violated’. The Commission expressed the opinion that there had been breach of paragraph 2 of the Convention (art. 6-2) (nine votes to six, with one abstention). The report contains three dissenting opinions. The Government made “a final submission and a formal motion, namely that the Court, when considering this matter, come to the conclusion that there was no violation of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms’

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and the Government of the Republic of Austria. The case originated in an application against this State lodged with the Commission on [DATE_TIME] under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention by an [NRP] citizen, Mr. [PERSON]. The Commission's request and the government's application were lodged within the period of [Date_TIME) laid down in Articles 32 par. 1 and [D date. 1). Their purpose is to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6. 1, 2 and 3 (d) ( art. 6-1, art.6-2, 6-3-d) The oral hearings took place in public at [LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. Immediately before their opening, the Court had held a preparatory meeting at which it had authorised the person assisting the Delegate of the Commission to address the Court in German (Rule 27 par. 3). There appeared before the Court: Mr. [PERSON], Ambassador, Ministry or Foreign Affairs, Agent, Advocate-General, Ministry of Justice, Mr. Oberrat, Federal Chancellery, Constitutional Department, Advisers; and the applicant's lawyer before the Commission. The Court heard addresses by the Government and by the Commission, as well as their replies to questions put by the Court. The applicant, an [NRP] citizen born in [DATE_TIME], lives in [LOCATION] where he practises the profession of accountant and financial consultant ([PERSON) He denies the facts alleged against him and denounced the complaint as being knowingly false. He says the object alleged to have caused the injury was, in fact, an envelope containing a single key. He claims he had wanted to give it back to Mrs. [PERSON], but it had slipped out of his hand and touched her arm. He said she had picked it up and thrown it, just above his head, over a distance of thirteen metres in the direction of his house. The District Court assessed the costs of that opinion on [DATE_TIME]. The district prosecutor requested the District Court to “decide that the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code [were] fulfilled“ (see paragraph 22 below) The Court acceded to the request by inserting in the file a note worded as follows: “B” (Beschluss, decision): “... the proceedings are closed pursuant to section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure“. Mr. [PERSON] denied that he had injured Mrs. ERSON, whether by throwing a bunch of keys or otherwise, and contested the doctor's findings. The District Court of Innsbruck has decided against Dr. [PERSON] for the offence of inflicting bodily harm. A quarrel between the two led to an envelope containing a key being thrown in the direction of a woman. The key struck the woman's hand, causing a superficial abrasion, and then bounced against the left side of the above-named person's chest. The District Court decided that the incident was insignificant and that the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code are met. The applicant challenged this decision before the Regional Court (Landesgericht) of [LOCATION] which, on [DATE_TIME), declared the appeal inadmissible. The Generalprokurator (the public prosecutor attached to the Supreme Court) filed an application for annulment of the decision dated [DATE_TIME] in the interests of the proper application of the law. He drew a distinction between the termination of proceedings by virtue of section 451 par. 2 and their termination by virtue. of section 90 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The former provision applied when, prior to the trial hearing, the court was satisfied that the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code were met; where, however, no sufficient grounds existed for continuing with the prosecution. In both cases, he said, the decisions would be taken without the formal hearing of evidence. The Generalprokurator moved the Supreme Court to hold that the Innsbruck District Court's decision dated [DATE_TIME] was contrary to the law, that is to say section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure read in conjunction with Article 6 par. 1 and 2 (art. 6-1 and 6-2) of the Convention. Mr. [PERSON] criticised the District Court for having failed to satisfy himself, before bringing the proceedings to a close, that the conditions stipulated under section 42 of the Penal Code are met. In order to do this, the applicant contended, the judge must have regard to all the evidence adduced and not simply to the evidence supporting the suspicion. The Supreme Court rejected the application for annulment on [DATE_TIME]. In the opinion of the Supreme Court, the application of section 42 par. 1 of the Penal Code did not place the suspect in a worse position than where the case is closed for some other reason. Section 42 is not at all meant to be used to terminate proceedings when it is certain that an offence cannot be proved on the facts or does not exist in law. Even if a court describes the suspect's conduct in terms of findings of fact, any statements to this effect could not be regarded as judicial findings. The person concerned has no right to have doubtful issues in the case clarified. The judgment of the Supreme Court was reproduced in an [NRP] legal journal but the applicant's identity was not revealed. Legal proof of the suspect's guilt is not the object pursued under section 42 of the Penal Code. No question arises as to the extent to which a decision given in pursuance of this provision has or has not been preceded by proceedings complying with the requirements of Article 6 par. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. The costs of the procedure, and notably the costs of a medical opinion, were borne by the State. The applicant himself had to pay his lawyer's fees and his own expenses. The public prosecutor may have preliminary enquiries carried out by the investigating judge, the district courts and the police authorities. In district court proceedings there is no formal process of investigation and no special procedure of accusation. All that is required is a written or oral application from the district prosecutor seeking the imposition of a penalty on the person concerned. If sufficient grounds for prosecuting the individual in question are lacking, the public prosecutor shall take no further action on the complaint and shall transmit the file to the investigatingJudge, together with a statement to the effect that he sees no reason to continue with the prosecution. The judge must then terminate the preliminary enqu inquiries (section 90 par. 1). Section 42 was introduced into the new Austrian Penal Code which entered into force on [DATE_TIME], and is aimed at avoiding criminal trials in trivial cases. The Supreme Court and the great majority of legal commentators regard it as a clause which is not concerned with mere procedure but which provides a substantive ground for exonerating the accused. A decision taken by a court in pursuance of section 42 to terminate proceedings is not entered in the criminal record of the person concerned. The file relating to a case closed in this manner may be used in other legal (and disciplinary) proceedings, as may, in principle, the case-file in any legal action whatever its outcome. The Commission accepted the application on [DATE_TIME]. He claimed that this decision was contrary to Article 6 par. 2 (art. 6-2) of the Convention as it contained findings both on the facts of the alleged offence and on his guilt. In his submission, since such findings were required by the very terms of section 42 of the Penal Code, the legislation itself was inconsistent with Article 6Par. 2. He further alleged violation of the rights guaranteed by Article 6par. 1 and 3 (d) (art, 6-1 and 6-3-d) in that, notwithstanding his denial of the accusations made against him and his request for the hearing of witnesses in his favour, the District Court took its decision.

The [PERSON] case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and the Government of the Republic of Austria. The case originated in an application against this State lodged with the Commission on [DATE_TIME] under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention by an [NRP] citizen. The request refers to Articles 44 and [DATED_TIME) and to the declaration by [LOCATION] recognising the Court's compulsory jurisdiction. The Government's application asks the Court in particular to find that there has been no such breach in this case. Their purpose is to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations. President of the Chamber [PERSON] assumed office on [DATE_TIME] He ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government and of the Delegate of the Commission regarding the procedure to be followed. He decided that the Agent should have until [Date_TIME) to file a memorial and that the Delegates should be entitled to file in reply. Those appearing before the Court filed several documents during the hearings. The Government produced a document to the Court. The Court heard addresses by Mr. [Person] for the Government. The applicant's lawyer before the Commission, assisting the delegate, also appeared before the court. The applicant, an [NRP] citizen born in [DATE_TIME], lives in [LOCATION] where he practises the profession of accountant and financial consultant ([PERSON) The applicant denied the facts alleged against him and denounced the complaint as being knowingly false. He claimed that the object alleged to have caused the injury was, in fact, an envelope containing a single key. He said that he had wanted to give it back to Mrs. [PERSON], but it had slipped out of his hand and touched her arm. This note, he stated was available to the court, as an item for inclusion in the case-file. The Court registered the case on [DATE_TIME]. Under the heading “punishable act’ it specified “section 83 of the Penal Code’. Following receipt of the doctor's opinion, the District Court assessed the costs of that opinion. Mr. [PERSON] denied that he had injured Mrs. ERSON, whether by throwing a bunch of keys or otherwise. He requested that fresh medical evidence be taken forthwith. The proceedings were terminated on an unspecified date in pursuance of section 451 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court acceded to the request by inserting in the file a note worded as follows: “B“ (Beschluss) District Court of Innsbruck, Section 9, [DATE_TIME]. Dr. [PERSON] was accused of inflicting bodily harm on a civil party. The civil party alleged that the accused had caused her an injury, namely a bruise on her left arm and another below her left breast, with a bunch of keys. No injury could be established on the chest. The injury found (festgestellte) is insignificant. The fault (Verschulden) of the accused may be described as insignificant (geringfügig) and his character gives cause to expect that he will conduct himself properly in future. Therefore the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code are met. The Generalprokurator (the public prosecutor attached to the Supreme Court) filed an application for annulment of the decision dated [DATE_TIME] in the interests of the proper application of the law. He drew a distinction between the termination of. proceedings by virtue of section 451 par. 2 and their termination by virtue. of section 90 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The former provision applied when, prior to the trial hearing, the court was satisfied that the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code were met. Where, however, no sufficient grounds existed for continuing with the prosecution, the public prosecutor should close the file (zurücklegen) on the complaint. The Generalprokurator moved the Supreme Court to hold that the Innsbruck District Court's decision dated [DATE_TIME] was contrary to the law, that is to say section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure read in conjunction with Article 6 par. 1 and 2 (art. 6-1 and 6-2) of the Convention. Mr. [PERSON] criticised the District Court for having failed to satisfy himself, before bringing the proceedings to a close, that the conditions stipulated under section 42 of the Penal Code are met. The applicant contended that the judge must have regard to all the evidence adduced and not simply to the evidence supporting the suspicion. He alleged a breach of Article 6 par. 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention. He called on the Supreme Court to find infringements of the law. The Supreme Court rejected the application for annulment on [DATE_TIME]. In the opinion, the application of the Penal Code did not place the suspect in a worse position than where the case is closed for some other reason. The person concerned has no right to have doubtful issues in the case clarified. Section 42 simply requires the existence of a suspicion. Even if a court describes the suspect's conduct in terms of findings of fact, any statements to this effect could not be regarded as judicial findings. Any such decision contains a negative ruling on the merits of the case. The applicant's identity was not revealed. Legal proof of the suspect's guilt is not the object pursued under section 42 of the Penal Code. No question arises as to the extent to which a decision given in pursuance of this provision has or has not been preceded by proceedings complying with the requirements of Article 6 par. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. The costs of the procedure, and notably the costs of a medical opinion, were borne by the State. The applicant himself had to pay his lawyer's fees and his own expenses. The professional association to which Mr. [PERSON] belongs has not instituted any disciplinary proceedings against him. In district court proceedings there is no formal process of investigation and no special procedure of accusation. All that is required is a written or oral application from the district prosecutor seeking the imposition of a penalty on the person concerned. If sufficient grounds for prosecuting the individual in question are lacking, the public prosecutor shall take no further action on the complaint and shall transmit the file to the investigating judge, together with a statement to the effect that he sees no reason to continue with the prosecution. The judge must then terminate the preliminary enquiries (section 90 par. 1). This provision applies, mutatis mutandis, toDistrict court proceedings. In cases before a district court, the decision terminating proceedings is governed by section 451 par. 2. Section 42 was introduced into the new Austrian Penal Code which entered into force on [DATE_TIME], and is aimed at avoiding criminal trials in trivial cases. The Supreme Court and the great majority of legal commentators regard it as a clause which is not concerned with mere procedure but which provides a substantive ground for exonerating the accused. A decision taken by a court in pursuance of section 42 to terminate proceedings is not entered in the criminal record of the person concerned. The file relating to a case closed in this manner may be used in other legal (and disciplinary) proceedings, as may, in principle, the case-file in any legal action whatever its outcome. The Government contested these assertions, save apparently as regards the possibility of having access to the register of names. The Government requested the Court ‘to hold that in the present case the provisions of paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 (d) of Article 6 were not violated’ The Commission expressed the opinion that there had been breach of paragraph 2 (art. 6-2) (nine votes to six, with one abstention). The report contains three dissenting opinions. The Government made “a final submission and a formal motion, namely that the Court, when considering this matter, come to the conclusion that there was no violation of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms in all three aspects which have been mentioned“.

PROCEDURE

The [PERSON] case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) and the Government of the Republic of Austria (“the Government“). The case originated in an application against this State lodged with the Commission on [DATE_TIME] under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention by an [NRP] citizen, Mr. [PERSON].

The Commission's request and the Government's application were lodged with the registry of the Court, within the period of [DATE_TIME] laid down in Articles 32 par. 1 and [DATE_TIME] (art. 32-1, art. 47), on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] respectively. The request refers to Articles 44 and [DATE_TIME] (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration by [LOCATION] recognising the Court's compulsory jurisdiction (Article 46) (art. 46), while the application refers to Article 48 (art. 48). Their purpose is to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 par. 1, 2 and 3 (d) (art. 6-1, art. 6-2, art. 6-3-d) of the Convention; the Government's application asks the Court in particular to find that there has been no such breach in this case.

The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr. [PERSON], the President of the Court (Rule 21 par. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court). On [DATE_TIME] in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the five other members, namely Mr. [PERSON], Mr. [PERSON], Mr. [PERSON], Mr. [PERSON] and Sir [PERSON] (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 par. 4 of the Rules of Court) (art. 43). Subsequently, Mr. [PERSON], who was unable to attend, was replaced by the first substitute judge, Mr. L.-E. [PERSON] (Rules 22 and 24 par. 1).

Mr. [PERSON] assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 par. 5). He ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government and of the Delegate of the Commission regarding the procedure to be followed. On [DATE_TIME], he decided that the Agent should have until [DATE_TIME] to file a memorial and that the Delegate should be entitled to file a memorial in reply within [DATE_TIME] from the date of the transmission of the Government's memorial to him by the Registrar. The Government's memorial was received at the registry on [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME], the Secretary to the Commission advised the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearings, and forwarded to him the observations of the applicant's lawyer on the Government's memorial.

After consulting, through the Deputy Registrar, the Agent of the Government and the Delegate of the Commission, the President directed on [DATE_TIME] that the oral hearings should open on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME], the Government produced a document to the Court.

The oral hearings took place in public at [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. Immediately before their opening, the Court had held a preparatory meeting at which it had authorised the person assisting the Delegate of the Commission to address the Court in German (Rule 27 par. 3). There appeared before the Court:

for the Government: Mr. [PERSON], Ambassador, Ministry or Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr. [PERSON], Advocate-General, Ministry of Justice, Mr. [PERSON], Oberrat, Federal Chancellery, Constitutional Department, Advisers;

for the Commission: Mr. [PERSON], [LOCATION], Mr. [PERSON], the applicant's lawyer before the Commission, assisting the Delegate (Rule 29 par. 1, second sentence, of the Rules of Court). The Court heard addresses by Mr. [PERSON], Mr. [PERSON] and Mr. [PERSON] for the Government and by Mr. [PERSON] and Mr. [PERSON] for the Commission, as well as their replies to questions put by the Court. Those appearing before the Court filed several documents during the hearings.

On [DATE_TIME], acting on the instructions of the President, the Registrar asked the Agent of the Government to produce two documents; those documents were received at the registry on [DATE_TIME].

AS TO THE FACTS

I. THE PARTICULAR CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant, an [NRP] citizen born in [DATE_TIME], lives in [LOCATION] where he practises the profession of accountant and financial consultant ([PERSON]).

On [DATE_TIME], an [DATE_TIME] woman, Mrs. [PERSON], acting through a lawyer, reported to the [LOCATION] public prosecutor's office that [DATE_TIME] during a quarrel Mr. [PERSON] had thrown at another person, Mrs. [PERSON], a bunch of keys which had then struck her (Mrs. [PERSON]), causing her injury. In her letter headed “request to inquire into a set of facts“, she called on the prosecutor's office to take criminal proceedings against the applicant and stated that she would be a civil party claiming damages in any such proceedings (Privatbeteiligte).

The federal police at [LOCATION], instructed on [DATE_TIME] by the public prosecutor's office to investigate whether or not a punishable act had been committed, interrogated several persons cited by Mrs. [PERSON] at witnesses and, on [DATE_TIME], the applicant himself. He denied the facts alleged against him and denounced the complaint as being knowingly false. After pointing out that the object alleged to have caused the injury was, in fact, an envelope containing a single key, he asserted, amongst other things, that he had not thrown it: he had wanted to give it back to Mrs. [PERSON], but it had slipped out of his hand and touched her arm. Mrs. [PERSON], he said, had picked it up and thrown it, just above his head, over a distance of thirteen metres in the direction of his house. Mr. [PERSON]'s wife and two employees had written a note setting out what they remembered of the incident. This note, he stated was available to the court, as an item for inclusion in the case-file. The police accepted the note, but did not question Mrs. [PERSON] or the employees. On [DATE_TIME], the public prosecutor's office, to which the file had been returned, asked the Innsbruck District Court ([PERSON]) to procure a medical report on the seriousness of Mrs. [PERSON]'s injury. The Court registered the case on [DATE_TIME]; under the heading “punishable act“ it specified “section 83 of the Penal Code“, which is a provision, amongst others, dealing with the infliction of bodily harm. Following receipt of the doctor's opinion, the District Court assessed the costs of that opinion on [DATE_TIME]. The district prosecutor ([PERSON]) requested the District Court on [DATE_TIME] to “decide that the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code [were] fulfilled“ (see paragraph 22 below). The Court acceded to the request on [DATE_TIME] by inserting in the file a note worded as follows: “B“ (Beschluss, decision): “... the proceedings are closed pursuant to section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure“; in addition, it added to the register, under the heading “date and manner ... of disposal of the matter“ (Erledigung): “24. 11. Section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure“.

On [DATE_TIME], an application was made to the District Court by Mr. [PERSON] who, after consultation of the file on his case, had come to learn on [DATE_TIME] of the submissions made by the public prosecutor's office on [DATE_TIME]; however, like that office, he was not aware of the decision of [DATE_TIME]. He denied that he had injured Mrs. [PERSON], whether by throwing a bunch of keys or otherwise, and contested the doctor's findings, claiming in particular that the latter had based his opinion on information that was contradicted by the material in the case-file (aktenwidrig). He called on the District Court either to acquit him after trial or to terminate the proceedings pursuant to section 90 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 21 below). He requested that, if the District Court should choose the first alternative, fresh medical evidence be taken forthwith. On [DATE_TIME], the District Court notified an associate of the applicant's lawyer that the proceedings had been terminated - on an unspecified date - in pursuance of section 451 2 the Code of Criminal Procedure. Following a request made by Mr. [PERSON] on [DATE_TIME], the Court served on him on [DATE_TIME] a decision dated [DATE_TIME] which reads as follows (translation from [NRP]): “Decision In the criminal case (Strafsache) against Dr. [PERSON] for the offence of inflicting bodily harm, within the meaning of section 83 of the Penal Code, the District Court of Innsbruck has decided as follows upon the request of the public prosecutor: The conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code are met; the proceedings are terminated in accordance with section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Reasons By letter of [DATE_TIME], the civil party [PERSON] informed the public prosecutor of an incident involving herself and the accused (Beschuldigter) which had happened on [DATE_TIME]. She alleged that the accused had caused her an injury, namely a bruise on her left arm and another below her left breast, with a bunch of keys. The investigations made thereupon and the expert opinion have shown (ergeben) that in the course of a quarrel the accused flew into a rage and threw an envelope containing a key in the direction of Mrs. [PERSON] who however managed to avoid the missile, while the [DATE_TIME] [PERSON] standing behind her was hit. The key first struck the back of the right hand, causing a superficial abrasion, and then bounced against the left side of the above-named person's chest. No injury could be established on the chest. The injury found (festgestellte) is insignificant (geringfügig) as it does not exceed the [DATE_TIME] limit; the fault (Verschulden) of the accused may be described as insignificant (geringfügig), and his character gives cause to expect that he will conduct himself properly in future. Therefore the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code are met, justifying the above decision. District Court of Innsbruck, Section 9, [DATE_TIME].“

The applicant challenged this decision before the Regional Court (Landesgericht) of [LOCATION] which, on [DATE_TIME], declared the appeal ([PERSON]) inadmissible on the ground that section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure limited the right of appeal to the prosecutor ([NRP]).

On [DATE_TIME], a little more than six months after the European Commission of Human Rights had accepted the application, the Generalprokurator (the public prosecutor attached to the Supreme Court ([PERSON]) filed, with the Supreme Court, pursuant to section 33 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an application for annulment of the decision dated [DATE_TIME] in the interests of the proper application of the law (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde zur Wahrung des Gesetzes). The Generalprokurator drew a distinction between the termination of proceedings by virtue of section 451 par. 2 and their termination by virtue of section 90 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The former provision applied when, prior to the trial hearing, the court was satisfied that the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code were met; where, however, no sufficient grounds existed for continuing with the prosecution, the public prosecutor should close the file (zurücklegen) on the complaint and the investigating judge should bring the proceeding to an end in accordance with the general rules laid down in section 90 par. 1 and 447 par. 1. In both cases, he said, the decisions would be taken without the formal hearing of evidence ([PERSON]), something which, as followed in any event from Article 6 par. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention - Article 6 par. 1 (art. 6-1) being a provision that has constitutional status in [NRP] law -, should in principle precede any finding of guilt (Schulderkenntnis). Thus, in the submission of the Generalprokurator, section 42 of the Penal Code was not appropriate where, on the basis of the complaint or the preliminary enquiries, no offence could be established on the facts or existed in law. On the other hand, for section 42 to apply it was not essential for there to be proof of guilt, but merely a suspicion ([PERSON]) such as would warrant the opening of preliminary enquiries or an application seeking the imposition of a penalty. A court decision terminating proceedings in accordance with section 42 could therefore only be grounded on a “suspected state of affairs“ (Verdachtslage) as disclosed by the case-file: the court had to limit itself to ascertaining whether there existed against the suspect sufficient suspicion for proceeding with the prosecution and whether, on the hypothetical assumption that the suspect had indeed committed the alleged offence, he was or was not entitled to benefit from the ground for exoneration ([LOCATION]) provided for under section 42 of the Penal Code. It seemed inadmissible to state in the reasons for such a decision conclusions on the objective and subjective aspects of the act and to take it as proved against the suspect that he had engaged in a certain course of conduct constituting a punishable act. Such an assertion in the reasons for a decision terminating proceedings amounted to a finding of guilt without any formal taking of evidence at a public hearing, which would be in violation of Article 6 par. 2 (art. 6-2) of the Convention. In the instant case, said the Generalprokurator, the District Court had clearly indicated that it accepted the account of the incident given by Mrs. [PERSON] and corroborated by the police investigations and by the medical evidence, and that it disbelieved the applicant's denials which were mainly concerned with what had happened during the incident (Tathergang). He submitted that as the decision in issue was not capable of causing Mr. [PERSON] any direct prejudice, a finding that it had infringed the law would be sufficient. The Generalprokurator therefore moved the Supreme Court to hold that the Innsbruck District Court's decision dated [DATE_TIME] was, as regards its reasoning, contrary to the law, that is to say section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure read in conjunction with Article 6 par. 1 and 2 (art. 6-1, art. 6-2) of the Convention.

On [DATE_TIME], Mr. [PERSON] submitted to the Supreme Court certain observations on the application for annulment. Whilst welcoming the initiative taken by the Generalprokurator, he considered that the latter had disregarded essential elements of violation of the law inherent in the impugned decision. In particular, he disputed the interpretation given by the Generalprokurator to section 42 of the Penal Code; in the applicant's view, this section in fact required the court to make a positive finding of an act fulfilling the description of a criminal offence. He relied on section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which places the judge under a duty to satisfy himself, before bringing the proceedings to a close, that the conditions stipulated under section 42 of the Penal Code are met; in order to do this, so the applicant contended, the judge must have regard to all the evidence adduced and not simply to the evidence supporting the suspicion. Mr. [PERSON] criticised the District Court for having failed to take into consideration evidence in his favour, for having declined to hear witnesses requested by him and for not having given him the opportunity to challenge the expert medical opinion; he alleged a breach of Article 6 par. 1 and 3 (d) (art. 6-1, art. 6-3-d) of the Convention. He accordingly called on the Supreme Court to find infringements of the law other than those pleaded by the Generalprokurator and to order that the proceedings be terminated under section 451 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The Supreme Court rejected the application for annulment on [DATE_TIME]. In the opinion of the Supreme Court, the application of section 42 par. 1 of the Penal Code did not place the suspect in a worse position than where the case is closed for some other reason (for example, in pursuance of section 90 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure), that is to say, a closure of the case which, in general, does not involve establishing the innocence of the person concerned. Section 42 is not at all meant to be used to terminate proceedings when it is certain that an offence cannot be proved on the facts or does not exist in law. On the other hand, section 42 does not demand verification of the objective and subjective elements of the offence; indeed, this would be contrary to the main object of the section, namely procedural economy (Prozessökonomie - the principle that the court's time should be usefully employed). The person concerned thus has no right to have doubtful issues in the case clarified. Section 42 simply requires the existence of a suspicion. Even if a court describes the suspect's conduct in terms of findings of fact, any statements to this effect could not be regarded as judicial findings ([PERSON]), within the meaning of section 270 par. 2, no. 5, of the Code of Criminal Procedure, with the attendant legal consequences. In point of fact, by reason of its basic legal character, any decision taken in pursuance of section 42 of the Penal Code can only be understood in one way: further clarification of, and possible prosecution in, a case which is already recognisable as being a trifling matter is to be avoided, not least in the interests of procedural economy. Howsoever the reasons given therefore may be worded, any such decision contains - if only because of its very nature - a negative ruling on the merits of the case and does not at all amount to a declaration, equivalent to a finding of guilt, that the suspect has (unlawfully and with criminal intent) committed a punishable act. It would certainly have been preferable had the Innsbruck District Court stated this explicitly and without ambiguity in the decision being challenged. Nonetheless, the more or less apposite choice of wording in the reasoning could not deprive the reasoning of the specific significance it had as a result of the nature of the decision given and could not, therefore, in any way adversely affect the person concerned. Since legal proof of the suspect's guilt is not the object pursued under section 42 of the Penal Code, no question arises as to the extent to which a decision given in pursuance of this provision has or has not been preceded by proceedings complying with the requirements of Article 6 par. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention.

The judgment of the Supreme Court was reproduced in an [NRP] legal journal but the applicant's identity was not revealed. The accompanying commentary on the judgment referred to an article entitled “A trivial affair leads to an application against [LOCATION]“ (“Aus Bagatellsache wurde Klage gegen Österreich“), which had been published in a newspaper in [DATE_TIME] and which did disclose his name, profession and place of residence. The professional association to which Mr. [PERSON] belongs has not instituted any disciplinary proceedings against him in respect of the facts underlying Mrs. [PERSON]'s complaint. According to Mr. [PERSON], the file on his case, including the Innsbruck District Court's decision dated [DATE_TIME], has been produced in evidence in a civil action between himself and Mrs. [PERSON] in the matter of an easement ([PERSON]); an order issued by the competent civil court in [LOCATION] took the case-file into consideration.

The costs of the procedure, and notably the costs of the medical opinion, were borne by the State. The applicant himself had to pay his lawyer's fees and his own expenses.

II. THE RELEVANT LEGISLATION

In [LOCATION], the public prosecutor ([PERSON]) is required by law to inquire into the correctness of any report (Anzeige) of an offence for which a prosecution must be brought as a matter of course (section 87 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure). He is obliged, as a matter of course, to prosecute in respect of any offence which appears to him to have been committed and where it is not a precondition of investigation and punishment that an application be made by the victim or some other person concerned; it is his duty to cause the competent court to take the necessary measures of investigation and punishment (section 34 par. 1). In order to procure the necessary evidence for the institution of criminal proceedings or for the closing of the file (Zurücklegung) on a complaint, the public prosecutor may have preliminary enquiries ([PERSON]) carried out by the investigating judge, the district courts and the police authorities (section 88 par. 1).

Where the public prosecutor is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for bringing a criminal prosecution, he shall either apply for the institution of a preliminary investigation ([LOCATION]) or file a formal accusation (Anklageschrift, section 90 par. 1). However, in district court proceedings there is no formal process of investigation and no special procedure of accusation: all that is required is a written or oral application from the district prosecutor seeking the imposition of a penalty on the person concerned ([PERSON], section 451 par. 1).

Where sufficient grounds for prosecuting the individual in question are lacking, the public prosecutor shall take no further action on the complaint and shall transmit the file to the investigating judge, together with a statement to the effect that he sees no reason to continue with the prosecution; the judge must then terminate the preliminary enquiries (section 90 par. 1). This provision applies, mutatis mutandis, to district court proceedings (section 447 par. 1). Under the terms of section 90 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the public prosecutor may alternatively ask the investigating judge to hold that the conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code are met. In cases before a district court, the decision terminating proceedings is governed by section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provides (translation from [NRP]): “If the court is satisfied that the conditions laid down in section 42 are met, it shall terminate the proceedings by a decision. The public prosecutor may lodge an appeal against any such decision ...“

Section 42 of the Penal Code reads as follows (translation from [NRP]): “(1) Where an act requiring public prosecution as a matter of course involves liability to no more than a fine, a custodial sentence not exceeding [DATE_TIME] or both, the act shall not be punishable (strafbar) if

1. the guilt ([PERSON]) of the author of the act is slight (gering);

2. the act has had no or only trifling consequences, and if addition

punishment is not necessary in order to deter the author of the act or other persons from committing criminal offences. (2) The decision whether or not the conditions of paragraph (1) hereof are met shall be taken by the court; where the court decides in the affirmative, it shall bring the proceedings to a close no matter what stage they may have reached.“ Section 42 was introduced into the new Austrian Penal Code which entered into force on [DATE_TIME], and is aimed at avoiding criminal trials in trivial cases, notably for reasons of procedural economy; the section is headed “acts not meriting punishment“ (“mangelnde [PERSON]“). The Supreme Court and the great majority of legal commentators regard it as a clause which is not concerned with mere procedure but which provides a substantive ground for exonerating the accused (sachlicher [LOCATION]).

A decision taken by a court in pursuance of section 42 to terminate proceedings is not entered in the criminal record of the person concerned. The file relating to a case closed in this manner may be used in other legal (and disciplinary) proceedings, as may, in principle, the case-file in any legal action whatever its outcome. According to Mr. [PERSON], anyone may go to the court and consult the register of cases and the register of names and, at least as far as the former is concerned, ask for an extract. The Government contested these assertions, save apparently as regards the possibility of having access to the register of names. The latter simply contains a reference to the register of cases without giving any indication as to the nature of the litigation.

As a result of the present case, two circulars were issued on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] by the relevant [NRP] authorities drawing the attention of the courts to the problems raised by the application of section 42 of the Penal Code and to the need for a careful wording of the relevant decisions (see paragraphs 33 and 34 of the report of the Commission). PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE COMMISSION

In his application of [DATE_TIME] to the Commission (no. 8269/78), Mr. [PERSON] complained of the Innsbruck District Court's decision dated [DATE_TIME]. He claimed that this decision was contrary to Article 6 par. 2 (art. 6-2) of the Convention as it contained findings both on the facts of the alleged offence and on his guilt. In his submission, since such findings were required by the very terms of section 42 of the Penal Code, the legislation itself was inconsistent with Article 6 par. 2 (art. 6-2). He further alleged violation of the rights guaranteed by Article 6 par. 1 and 3 (d) (art. 6-1, art. 6-3-d) in that, notwithstanding his denial of the accusations made against him and his request for the hearing of witnesses in his favour, the District Court took its decision without holding a trial hearing and without proper inquiry into the evidence.

The Commission accepted the application on [DATE_TIME]. In its report of [DATE_TIME] (Article 31 of the Convention) (art. 31), the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been breach of paragraph 2 of Article 6 (art. 6-2) (nine votes to six, with one abstention), but no breach of paragraph 1 or paragraph 3 (d) (art. 6-1, art. 6-3-d) (twelve votes to three, with one abstention). The report contains three dissenting opinions. FINAL SUBMISSIONS MADE TO THE COURT BY THE GOVERNMENT

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26390/95) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that certain criminal proceedings against him in relation to fraud charges had exceeded a reasonable time. According to the [NRP] courts’ findings in the proceedings referred to below, the business was a fraudulent pyramid scheme. The Court decided the case on the basis of the case-file as it stood. The application was transferred to the Court on [DATE_TIME], when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. Consumer Ombudsman filed a complaint with the Director General of Public Prosecutions. Payments were made to a company in [LOCATION]. No goods containing the cultivated substances were ever marketed or produced. The companies went into bankruptcy in [DATE_TIME]. The police received 335 complaints from cultivators in various parts of [LOCation]. Further complaints were made by a major bank and the tax authorities. The police interviewed the applicant as a witness, because of his role in the companies. The Probate Court (skifteretten) received the final report from the administrators of the companies of [PERSON] The applicant was arrested but released on certain conditions. One of the two leading figures in the criminal activity concerned, Mr D.R., disappeared. A search for him with an arrest warrant was made via Interpol. He was arrested by the [NRP] police and extradited to Oslo. The City Court convicted the applicant of all but the VAT charges, and sentenced him to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment. The court noted from the outset that the offences for which the applicant was convicted were punishable by imprisonment. It further stated that general considerations of crime prevention suggested that economic factors should be taken into account when sentencing the applicant. The case was heard at the Oslo City Court on [Date_TIME].  Oslo City Court found the defendants’ conduct particularly reprehensible. Two other co-defendants, including Mr D.R., who were considered to have played a more prominent role in the proscribed activity, were sentenced to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment. The applicant sought to appeal to the Supreme Court, alleging a procedural error in the first instance proceedings and requesting a new trial. The Supreme Court rejected the appeal on the procedural matter. As regards sentencing, it recalled that the City Court said that the offences of the kind at issue warranted a severe penalty. ... In the court’s view, had greater caution been displayed, the pyramid scheme would have been revealed earlier. The Supreme Court held that although more time had elapsed since the City Court’s judgment, it saw no reason for reducing the sentence. The Supreme Court. had taken into consideration as a mitigating circumstance the long time which had elapsed. since the incriminated conduct. The court. had also taken into. consideration as an aggravating circumstance the length of time since the. incriminating conduct had taken place. The Court. held that the sentence was not reduced because of the fact that more time. had elapsed since the.
