PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 27992/06) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national, Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON] of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that his pre-trial detention had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention; that the domestic courts had failed to examine “speedily” one of his appeals against the extension of the detention and one of his requests for release; that his detention had been unlawful; and that the length of criminal proceedings in his case had been excessive.

On [DATE_TIME] the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the complaints under Article 5 § 3 and 5 § 4 of the Convention to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed several offences of drug trafficking.

On [DATE_TIME] the Szczecin District Court remanded him in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences in question. It also considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that he might tamper with evidence and go into hiding. The court also stressed the severity of the anticipated sentence.

In the course of the investigation, his detention was extended several times. In their decisions the courts referred to the reasons previously given and the likelihood that he had committed the offences in an organised criminal group. Further, they referred to the complexity of the case and the fact that many suspects were involved and some of them had not yet been arrested. They stressed that the detention was justified by the need to analyse the existing evidence and the scope of the applicant’s criminal activity, as well as the necessity to obtain further evidence, in particular to have witnesses examined.

The applicant appealed against the decision extending his detention (he appealed against the Szczecin District Court’s decisions of [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]) but to no avail. His applications for release were likewise unsuccessful.

However, on [DATE_TIME] the Szczecin Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy), after examination of the applicant’s appeal, amended the decision extending his detention given by the Szczecin District Court on [DATE_TIME] and reduced the detention period by [DATE_TIME]. The court criticised the manner in which the investigation and the case file had been conducted, as well as pointing out shortcomings in the prosecutor’s request for extension of the applicant’s detention.

On [DATE_TIME] the investigation was completed and on [DATE_TIME] the applicant and other suspects were indicted before the court.

The detention was then subsequently extended by the Szczecin District Court on several occasions.

In a decision given on [DATE_TIME], the Szczecin District Court extended the applicant’s detention and the detention of the other nine co‑accused until [DATE_TIME]. However, at the same time it ruled that the applicant could be released on bail on payment of a security of 30,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. 7,500 euros (EUR). The court noted also that “in most cases the accused were charged with acting in an organised criminal group or possibly (ewentualnie) the offences with which they were charged had been committed together and under arrangement with other persons”. The court did not however indicate which of the accused had been involved in the criminal group.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant’s defence counsel requested the court to lower the amount of bail by PLN 10,000, but his request was rejected on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant did not pay the security and his detention was extended beyond the statutory [DATE_TIME] time-limit by the Szczecin Court of Appeal ([PERSON]) on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME].

In the decision of [DATE_TIME], which considered the extension of the detention only in relation to the applicant, the court did not mention the charge of acting in an organised criminal group. It noted however that “the applicant was charged with two offences and in one case the anticipated penalty exceeded [DATE_TIME] imprisonment. In such a situation there is ipso iure a presumption that the applicant would obstruct the proceedings because of the fear of a severe sentence” ([PERSON] na [NRP] przed grożąca [PERSON]).

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant lodged an appeal against the decision of [DATE_TIME] and on [DATE_TIME] he applied for release. According to the applicant, neither the appeal against the extension of his detention nor the application for release was examined. In their observations the Government submitted that the applicant’s appeal of [DATE_TIME] had been examined by the Szczecin Court of Appeal on [DATE_TIME] and dismissed. They failed however to submit the relevant documents. As regards the applicant’s request for release of [DATE_TIME], the Government admitted that, “by mistake” it had not been examined by the court.

On [DATE_TIME] the Szczecin Court of Appeal extended the applicant’s detention until [DATE_TIME]. The court relied on the same grounds as previously and reiterated the argument of the Szczecin District Court of [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 13 above) namely that “most of the co-accused” had been charged with acting in an organised criminal group.

On [DATE_TIME] the Szczecin District Court sentenced the applicant to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment and ordered his release. It appears that he was released on [DATE_TIME].

On an unspecified date the applicant appealed against the first‑instance judgment. The proceedings are pending before the appellate court.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 1955/10) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national, Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant was represented by Mr [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOCATION]. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, [PERSON] of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The applicant alleged that his right to respect for family life and his right to marry and found a family had been breached.

On [DATE_TIME] the application was communicated to the Government. The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the admissibility and merits. In addition, [PERSON] comments were received from the European Centre for Justice and Human Rights (Centre européen pour la justice et [PERSON]), which had been given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 3 of the Rules of Court).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION].

In [DATE_TIME] the applicant married R. In [DATE_TIME] R. underwent infertility treatment so she could conceive a child with him.

In [DATE_TIME] the applicant met A.H. In [DATE_TIME] he moved out of the flat he had lived in with [NRP]

On [DATE_TIME] A.H. gave birth to their daughter, M.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant filed a petition for divorce. At first he requested a no-fault divorce. In his petition the applicant referred to various marital misunderstandings and quarrels for which he blamed the respondent. He admitted that he had moved out of the matrimonial home, but did not mention his involvement with a new partner.

At a hearing held on [DATE_TIME] the applicant refused to undergo the mediation process provided for by divorce law. R. did not agree to a divorce, declared that she loved the applicant and asked the court to dismiss the divorce petition.

Subsequently, the applicant requested a divorce on fault‑based grounds.

During the proceedings thirteen witnesses were heard. Most of them were of the opinion that the marriage seemed happy until [DATE_TIME]. Only the applicant’s mother, his two colleagues and his cousin recalled minor arguments between the spouses.

During the final hearing on [DATE_TIME] the respondent reiterated her refusal to divorce.

On [DATE_TIME] the Lublin Regional Court refused to grant the divorce to the applicant. The court held that he was the only person responsible for the breakdown of his marriage because he had failed to respect the obligation of fidelity. The court did not find it credible that problems had already begun within [DATE_TIME] of the marriage. It observed that until [DATE_TIME] the applicant had not wanted children. In [DATE_TIME] he had changed his mind. For that reason [PERSON] had undergone surgery, the operation having taken place in [DATE_TIME].

The marital situation had subsequently changed when the applicant had met [PERSON] He had no longer wished to have a child with his wife. The court noted contradictions between the testimony given by the applicant, who had referred to the alleged serious problems in marital life prior to [DATE_TIME] on the one hand, and the decision to treat R.’s infertility in [DATE_TIME] on the other. The respondent had been shocked by the applicant’s unfaithfulness and had been treated for depression since [DATE_TIME].

The court acknowledged that there had indeed been “a complete and irretrievable marriage breakdown” within the meaning of Article 56 § 1 of the Family and Guardianship Code. Reconciliation was unlikely as the applicant had consistently rejected all attempts made by R. to reconcile their differences. Moreover, he had been in a relationship with A.H. for [DATE_TIME] and had a child with her.

The court emphasised that under Article 56 § 3 of the Family and Guardianship Code, a divorce could not be granted if it had been requested by the party whose fault it was that the marriage had broken down, if the other party refused to consent and the refusal of the innocent party was not “contrary to the reasonable principles of social coexistence” ([PERSON] społecznego) within the meaning of Article 5 of the Civil Code.

The court considered that R.’s refusal to divorce should be presumed to be compatible with those universally accepted principles. It referred to the case-law of the Supreme Court to the effect that a refusal of consent to a divorce was to be presumed to be compliant with those principles unless there were case-specific indications to the contrary. There was no indication that when refusing to give her consent [PERSON] had acted out of hatred, was motivated by vengeance, or simply wanted to vex the applicant. The court emphasised that she had repeatedly stated during the proceedings that she was ready to reconcile with him despite the fact that he had a child with another woman.

The court stressed that the duration of the applicant’s new relationship could not by itself be considered to be a sufficient reason for granting the divorce.

The applicant appealed against the judgment. He argued, inter alia, that the court had erred in holding that a spouse’s refusal to consent to a divorce could be disregarded only when it was of an abusive nature or was dictated by hostility towards the spouse seeking the divorce. The court should have examined the negative social consequences caused by continuing the formal existence of failed marriages. In his case, it had failed to do so.

On [DATE_TIME] the Lublin Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

The applicant did not request to be served with the written grounds for the appellate judgment. The grounds were therefore not prepared.

The judgment was final, a cassation appeal against a divorce judgment not being available in law.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13378/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that the survivor of a married couple or a homosexual relationship registered under the Civil Partnership Act 2004 would be exempt from paying inheritance tax in these circumstances. The application was allocated to a Chamber within the Fourth Section of the Court. On [DATE_TIME] the Chamber unanimously declared the application admissible and delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation of Article 14 of. the Convention taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicants are unmarried sisters. They have lived together, in a stable, committed and mutually supportive relationship, all their lives. The house is owned by the applicants in their joint names. According to an expert valuation dated [DATE_TIME], the property was worth 425,000 pounds sterling (GBP), or GBP 550,000 if sold together with the adjoining land. The sisters also jointly own two other properties, worth GBP 325,000 in total. In addition, each sister owns in her sole name shares and other investments worth approximately GBP 150,000. Each has made a will leaving all her property to the other. Each sister’s one-half share was worth significantly more than the current exemption threshold for inheritance tax (see paragraph 13 below).

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 58453/00) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national, Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON], [LOCATION], and, subsequently, Mrs [PERSON], [PERSON], of the Federal Ministry of Justice.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal of child benefits [DATE_TIME] amounted to discrimination in the exercise of his right to respect for family life.

The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1.

By a decision of [DATE_TIME] the Court declared the application partly admissible.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1).

The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME]. At the time the application was lodged he lived in [LOCATION] in [LOCATION]. He currently resides in [LOCATION] in [LOCATION].

1. The applicant’s situation in [LOCATION]

The applicant immigrated to [LOCATION] in [DATE_TIME]. His request for asylum was rejected. His expulsion was, however, suspended under the agreement of the Home Secretaries of the Länder not to expel [NRP] nationals (“Ostblockbeschlüsse” der Innenminister der Länder). In [DATE_TIME] the applicant obtained a provisional residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis). In [DATE_TIME], following an amendment of the Aliens Act, he was issued with a limited residence title for exceptional purposes ([NRP]). This residence title was renewed [DATE_TIME], the last time in [DATE_TIME] until [DATE_TIME]. In [DATE_TIME] the applicant obtained an unlimited residence permit (Aufenthaltsberechtigung).

In [DATE_TIME] the applicant’s daughter was born.

2. The child benefit proceedings before the Labour Office

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant applied to the Aschaffenburg Labour Office (Arbeitsamt) for child benefits according to Section 1 of the Federal Child Benefits Act ([LOCATION], see relevant domestic law below).

On [DATE_TIME] the Labour Office dismissed the applicant’s request under Section 1 § 3 of the Child Benefits Act. It noted that the applicant only had a limited residence title for exceptional purposes, and no unlimited residence permit or provisional residence permit, as required under Section 1 § 3.

On [DATE_TIME] the Federal Labour Office (Bundesanstalt für Arbeit) rejected his objection.

3. The proceedings before the Social Court

The applicant lodged an action with the Würzburg Social Court (Sozialgericht), claiming that he had been residing in [LOCATION] since [DATE_TIME] and that he should, therefore, have the right to child benefits.

On [DATE_TIME] the Social Court dismissed the applicant’s action regarding child benefits [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]. It confirmed that only aliens with an unlimited residence permit or with a provisional residence permit were entitled to the payment of child benefits under Section 1 § 3 of the Child Benefits Act, as in force until [DATE_TIME]. According to the Social Court, the legislature had only intended to grant child benefits to aliens who were likely to stay in [LOCATION] on a permanent basis. Aliens with only a limited residence title for exceptional purposes were, however, not likely to stay. The court further pointed out that this distinction did not violate the German Basic Law. In the present case, the legislature had remained within its wide margin of appreciation in social law matters.

4. The appeal proceedings

On [DATE_TIME] the Bavarian Social Court of Appeal (Landessozialgericht) dismissed the applicant’s appeal to the extent that his claims under the Child Benefits Act until [DATE_TIME] were concerned. The Court of Appeal confirmed the lower court’s reasoning, noting that the applicant did not have a stable residence permit in [DATE_TIME], as his limited residence title for exceptional purposes had had to be renewed [DATE_TIME]. Likewise, referring to the wide margin of appreciation of the legislature, it took the view that Section 1 § 3 of the Federal Child Benefits Act was compatible with the Basic Law. In this respect, it considered that until [DATE_TIME] families had benefited from child benefits and tax deductions ([PERSON]) as a system of compensation (dualer [PERSON]). The applicant and his wife had paid taxes in [DATE_TIME] but had not obtained child benefits. In the court’s view, this taxation, not the refusal of child benefits, might have violated the Basic Law; however, it was not for the social courts to decide on that matter.

On [DATE_TIME] the Federal Social Court (Bundessozialgericht) dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint combined with a request for an interim measure. He claimed that the relevant provision of the Federal Child Benefits Act was discriminatory and racist, and violated his right to respect for his family life. In addition, he alleged that the refusal of his request for child benefits infringed the principle of social justice (Sozialstaatsprinzip) laid down in Article 20 § 4 of the Basic Law.

On [DATE_TIME] the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) refused to entertain his complaint and rejected his request for an interim measure.

5. The proceedings concerning claims after [DATE_TIME]

On [DATE_TIME] the Würzburg Social Court decided that it was not competent to deal with the applicant’s claims regarding child benefits for the period after [DATE_TIME] and transferred the proceedings to the Nuremberg Tax Court (Finanzgericht). The proceedings before the Tax Court are still pending.

PROCEDURE

The case was referred to the Court on [DATE_TIME] by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) and on [DATE_TIME] by the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and [LOCATION] (“the Government“), within the [DATE_TIME] period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. [DATE_TIME]) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on [DATE_TIME] by a [NRP] citizen, Mr [PERSON]. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and [DATE_TIME] (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby [LOCATION] recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46); the Government’s application referred to Article 48 (art. 48). The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (art. 6-3-c).

In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30).

On [DATE_TIME], the President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the case of Maxwell v. [LOCATION] (no. 31/[PHONE_NUMBER]) should be heard by the same Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr [PERSON], the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On [DATE_TIME], in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mrs [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON] (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43).

As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5), Mr [PERSON], acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and [DATE_TIME]). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s memorial on [DATE_TIME] and the Government’s memorial on [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the Government submitted their written reply to the applicant’s claims for just satisfaction under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. On [DATE_TIME] the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would not submit written observations in reply.

In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court:

for the Government Mr [PERSON], Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Lord [PERSON] of Earlsferry, QC, Lord Advocate, Mr [PERSON], Counsel, Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Advisers;

for the Commission Mr [PERSON], Delegate;

for the applicant [PERSON], QC, Counsel, [PERSON], Solicitor. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides, Lord [PERSON] and [PERSON] as well as replies to its questions.

AS TO THE FACTS

I. CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant, Mr [PERSON], is a [NRP] citizen born in [DATE_TIME]. He lives in [LOCATION], [LOCATION]. On [DATE_TIME] three masked men, armed with a shotgun and a knife, carried out a robbery at a post office in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], [LOCATION], in the course of which they assaulted three post-office employees. They also caused damage to a motor car. Following investigations, Mr [PERSON] and two other men were arrested and remanded in custody. The applicant was indicted on a charge of assault and armed robbery, a charge of wilful damage and three charges relating to firearms. [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] he stood trial in the High Court of Justiciary sitting in [LOCATION].

The applicant received legal aid for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial.

During the trial a prosecution witness, Mrs G., entered the courtroom prior to giving evidence and spoke to one of the applicant’s co-accused, against whom charges had been dropped. When Mrs [PERSON] was called to give evidence, the applicant’s counsel objected on the basis of her earlier presence in court. The trial judge adjourned the case and instructed prosecuting counsel to make further inquiries into the matter so that it could be determined whether Mrs [PERSON]’s attendance was due to any negligence or failure on the part of the Crown. Prosecuting counsel informed the judge that inquiries had revealed no fault on the part of anyone for whom the Crown bore responsibility. This was not disputed by the applicant’s counsel, who, moreover, was unable to give any indication as to how Mrs [PERSON]’s evidence could be affected by her earlier presence in court. The trial judge accordingly took the view that no injustice would be done by Mrs [PERSON]’s examination. Finding that the relevant legal conditions were satisfied (see paragraph 17 below), he therefore exercised his discretion and permitted her to give evidence. Subsequently, counsel for the applicant had the opportunity to cross-examine Mrs G. on the matter of her attendance in court. In her evidence, Mrs [PERSON] stated that the applicant had been at her home the evening before the robbery and had spoken of robbing the post office. The following morning he had left the house and returned later with a bag, in a state of nervousness. Other evidence against the applicant included the fact that a shotgun and various items stolen from the post office were found on the applicant’s premises. In addition, a different witness identified Mr [PERSON] as being one of the robbers and Mrs [PERSON]’s statement was supported by her [DATE_TIME] daughter.

The jury found the applicant guilty on all the charges. Taking account of his numerous previous convictions, the judge sentenced him to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant, through his solicitor, lodged an intimation of intention to appeal against conviction.

Mr [PERSON] instructed new solicitors, who asked a different counsel to advise on the prospects of an appeal and to draft a note of appeal. In his opinion dated [DATE_TIME] counsel stated his view that the only possible ground of appeal related to the “admissibility of the evidence of Mrs G.“ and to the question “that the trial judge erred in exercising discretion in allowing her to be present“. However, he conceded that he had not been provided with sufficient information to be able properly to base an opinion or to frame grounds of appeal. Notwithstanding this acknowledgement he did draft a note of appeal which contained six grounds, the first two of which concerned the trial judge’s decision to admit the witness. This note of appeal was filed by the applicant’s solicitors on [DATE_TIME].

Up to this point all the work had been covered by the legal aid granted for the trial. An application to extend legal aid to the appeal proceedings had been submitted in [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the Scottish Legal Aid Board (“the Board“) asked the applicant to provide an opinion from counsel on the prospects of success. The earlier opinion dated [DATE_TIME] was accordingly forwarded to the Board, together with a supplementary opinion from the same counsel dated [DATE_TIME]. In this latter opinion counsel reiterated the view that the appeal rested on the question whether Mrs [PERSON]’s evidence was admissible. However, he again stated that he had not been provided with sufficient material on which to assess the merits of the appeal. “I regret meantime I am unable to answer the fundamental question in this case“, he concluded.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant’s solicitors informed the Board by telephone that counsel had finally decided that he could not support the application for legal aid or the appeal; that they were of the same view; and that, consequently, they could no longer act for the applicant. The terms of that telephone call were confirmed in a letter dated [DATE_TIME] from the solicitors to the Board.

On [DATE_TIME] the Scottish Legal Aid Board notified Mr [PERSON]’s solicitors that his application for legal aid had been refused as the Board was not satisfied, as it was required to be under the relevant legislation (see paragraph 26 below), that he had substantial grounds for taking an appeal and that it was reasonable that he should receive legal aid. In a letter of [DATE_TIME] to the applicant the Board added that it could not see any merit in the appeal. Despite the advice of his solicitors and counsel, Mr [PERSON] decided to proceed with the appeal.

The applicant, who had no legal knowledge and had no assistance with his submissions, presented his own case on [DATE_TIME] before the High Court of Justiciary, sitting in [LOCATION] and acting as an appellate court. The Crown was represented by counsel. There is no indication in the record that the court required counsel for the Crown to address it.

The appeal court considered the first two grounds of appeal relating to Mrs G. and held that these were ill-founded and that the trial judge had approached the matter properly. As the applicant did not address the court on the remaining grounds of appeal, these were not considered by the court. It did however examine other points raised by the applicant, but reached “the clear conclusion that there was no miscarriage of justice in the case“. The appeal against conviction was unanimously dismissed.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was released pending trial.

On [DATE_TIME] the Diyarbakır Assize Court declared its lack of jurisdiction and transferred the applicant's case to the Diyarbakır Juvenile Court, holding that the applicant had been a minor at the time of the events.

The Inner Vienna District Court (Bezirksgericht Wien Innere Stadt) on [DATE_TIME] and the Vienna regional Civil Court (Landesgericht für [PERSON) acting as guardianship court declared the applicant partly responsible for assaults. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. The applicant was found. incapacitated (beschränkt entmündigt) and appointed an adviser (Beistand) for him. On [DATE_TIME] the District Court appointed a new adviser, who has acted as such since then. In the meantime, further prosecutions were brought against Mr [PERSON] for assaults on warders and fellow prisoners and for serious threats against judges. According to the psychiatrists who examined him, he was suffering from paranoia [NRP], which was equivalent to a mental illness and meant that he was not responsible for his acts. He was extremely aggressive and incapable of understanding that his behaviour was unlawful, and there was a risk that attendance at the trial could be affected. The court found that the charges against Mr [PERSON] had been proved and ordered him to be detained under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code. The court relied on the opinions of three psychiatrists who had each diagnosed paranoia [NRP] which at least had been equivalent to a mental illness. The Regional Court, relying on section 50 of the Hospitals Law, ordered that the detention should be continued and that the applicant should be transferred as a matter of urgency to a psychiatric hospital, so that the treatment he required could be carried out. The Vienna Court of Appeal, to which the applicant had appealed, held on [Criminal Code Article 429 (4)]. His appeal against this decision was dismissed by the Vienna Court of Appeal on [DATE_TIME]. The Supreme Court varied the judgment of the Review Chamber in part and quashed the detention order and remitted the case. The Regional Court found that the charges against him had been proved and ordered him to be. detained in an institution for mentally ill offenders under Article 21 (1) of. the Criminal Code. Pursuant to Article 428 (4), the Review. Chamber and the Court of. Appeal extended the detention of the applicant in question. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court, acting under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code, extended Mr [PERSON]’s detention, as a psychiatric report produced at the request of that court stated that he was a dangerous person. PROCEDURE

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) on [DATE_TIME], within the [DATE_TIME] period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 10533/83) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr [PERSON], a [NRP] national, on [DATE_TIME].

The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and [DATE_TIME] (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby [LOCATION] recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 (paras. 1, 3 and 4), 8, [DATE_TIME] and 13 (art. 3, art. 5-1, art. 5-3, art. 5-4, art. 8, art. 10, art. 13).

In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30).

The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr [PERSON], the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On [DATE_TIME], in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr [PERSON], Mr L.-E. [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON] (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON], substitute judges, subsequently replaced Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON], who were unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rules 22 para. 1 and 24 para. 1).

Mr [PERSON] assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5) and, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Austrian Government (“the Government“), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant on the organisation of the procedure (Rule 37 para. 1 and Rule 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s memorial, which incorporated his claims for just satisfaction (Article 50 of the Convention) (art. 50), on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the Government informed him that they would not be submitting a memorial.

On [DATE_TIME] Mr [PERSON] gave the applicant leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3).

In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court:

for the Government Mr [PERSON], Ambassador, Legal Adviser, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr [PERSON], Federal Chancellery, Mrs [PERSON], Federal Ministry of Justice, Advisers;

for the Commission Mr [PERSON], Delegate;

for the applicant Mr [PERSON], Rechtsanwalt, Counsel. The Court heard addresses by them.

AS TO THE FACTS

I. THE PARTICULAR CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

Mr [PERSON] is a [NRP] citizen who has lived in [LOCATION] since [DATE_TIME]. He currently resides in [LOCATION].

A. The proceedings

From [DATE_TIME] to 13 [DATE_TIME] he served two prison sentences in succession, following convictions pronounced by the Vienna Regional Criminal Court ([LOCATION] für [PERSON]) and confirmed in part by the Supreme Court ([PERSON]), inter alia for assaults on his wife, clients of his television repair business and public officials.

The Inner Vienna District Court (Bezirksgericht Wien Innere Stadt) on [DATE_TIME] and the Vienna Regional Civil Court (Landesgericht für [PERSON]), acting as guardianship court ([PERSON]), on [DATE_TIME] declared the applicant partly incapacitated (beschränkt entmündigt) and appointed an adviser (Beistand) for him. They did so on the basis of a psychiatrist’s report which had been drawn up following numerous complaints by him about prison conditions. On [DATE_TIME] the District Court appointed a new adviser, who has acted as such since then. According to a ruling of the guardianship court of [DATE_TIME], his position was equivalent as from [DATE_TIME] to that of a curator ([PERSON]) within the meaning of Article 273 (3), sub-paragraph 3, of the Civil Code (see paragraph 54 below).

In the meantime, further prosecutions were brought against Mr [PERSON] for assaults on warders and fellow prisoners and for serious threats against judges. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court ordered that once he had finished serving his sentence on [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 9 above) the applicant should remain in detention under Article 180 (2), sub-paragraphs 1 and 3, of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 40 below), as there was reason to fear that he might attempt to abscond and might commit other offences. The applicant unsuccessfully appealed to the Review Chamber (Ratskammer) of the Regional Court and to the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), whose rulings were given on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] respectively. The pre-trial detention (Untersuchungshaft) was confirmed by the presiding judge of the Regional Court on [DATE_TIME].

In accordance with the opinions of several experts, the presiding judge on [DATE_TIME] ordered Mr [PERSON]’s provisional placement (vorläufige [PERSON]) in an institution for mentally ill offenders (Article 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; see paragraph 44 below). The order was confirmed by the Review Chamber on [DATE_TIME] and the Court of Appeal on [DATE_TIME], and the applicant was transferred to the special prison at [LOCATION], [LOCATION].

According to the psychiatrists who examined him, he was suffering from paranoia [NRP], which was equivalent to a mental illness and meant that he was not responsible for his acts; he was extremely aggressive and incapable of understanding that his behaviour was unlawful, and there was a risk that attendance at the trial could harm his health. Following these reports, the public prosecutor’s office amended the indictment on [DATE_TIME] and now sought Mr [PERSON]’s detention rather than conviction. From that date the detention in issue was based on Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 44 below). The applicant’s appeal against the amended indictment was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on [DATE_TIME].

The hearing before the Regional Court took place on [DATE_TIME]. It had previously been necessary to adjourn a hearing arranged for [DATE_TIME] because the case-file had been lost, to adjourn a hearing of [DATE_TIME] because of the applicant’s request for further witnesses to be called, a hearing of [DATE_TIME] because the presiding judge was absent, one of [DATE_TIME] because fresh evidence had been produced, one of [DATE_TIME] because of mistakes in sending out summonses, and one of [DATE_TIME] because the applicant had spat in the presiding judge’s face, which had led to the indictment being amended (see paragraph 13 above). On [DATE_TIME] the court found that the charges against Mr [PERSON] had been proved and ordered him to be detained under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 45 below), on the grounds that he was dangerous and not criminally responsible for his acts. The court relied on the opinions of three psychiatrists who had each diagnosed paranoia [NRP] which from [DATE_TIME] at least had been equivalent to a mental illness.

The applicant brought an application for a declaration of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) to the Supreme Court. The Regional Court decided, however, that pending the decision he should remain provisionally detained under Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but in prison, on the psychiatrist’s recommendation.

On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court, relying on section 50 of the Hospitals Law, ordered that the detention should be continued and that the applicant should be transferred as a matter of urgency to a psychiatric hospital, so that the treatment he required could be carried out. Mr [PERSON] stayed there from [DATE_TIME] and was then returned to the prison. The Vienna Court of Appeal, to which the applicant had appealed, held on [DATE_TIME] that it had no jurisdiction: as Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was the only provision which could apply, it was for the Review Chamber of the Regional Court to hear the appeal.

On [DATE_TIME] the Review Chamber upheld the detention in issue. Applying Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, it ordered Mr [PERSON] to be sent to the [LOCATION] psychiatric hospital so that he could receive urgent medical and socio- and psycho-therapeutic treatment there, which was essential inter alia because of the hunger strike he had carried on since [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] he was admitted to ward 23 of that hospital, and stayed there until his release on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant’s appeal against this decision was dismissed by the Vienna Court of Appeal on [DATE_TIME].

In the meantime the Supreme Court had on [DATE_TIME] varied the judgment of [DATE_TIME] in part (see paragraphs 14-15 above), quashed the detention order and remitted the case to the Regional Court.

On [DATE_TIME] Mr Herczegfalvy requested his release. On [DATE_TIME] the investigating judge informed him that he continued to be detained in accordance with Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. At that judge’s request, the psychiatric hospital submitted a report dated [DATE_TIME] expressing the opinion that it was not possible to place the applicant in ordinary pre-trial detention, as his aggressive behaviour was still causing danger to those around him. Pursuant to Article 429 (4), the Review Chamber and the Court of Appeal extended the detention in question in [DATE_TIME].

After hearings on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court, to which the case had been remitted (see paragraph 18 above), found that the charges against Mr Herczegfalvy - which included further serious threats against a judge on [DATE_TIME] - had been proved and ordered him to be detained in an institution for mentally ill offenders under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code. It based its decision on the judgment of [DATE_TIME], the three psychiatric reports on which it had been based (see paragraph 14 above), and the opinions of the authors of the reports, who had appeared at the hearing and stated that despite certain improvements there had been no fundamental change in the situation. As the applicant had withdrawn his appeal and application for a declaration of nullity in writing on [DATE_TIME] and at a hearing on [DATE_TIME], the judgment was on the latter date declared binding by a final order (Endverfügung), which set the date of 1 [DATE_TIME] for the next judicial review of the detention (Article 25 (3) of the Criminal Code; see paragraph 46 below). The applicant subsequently challenged the validity of his declarations. He said that he had made them only with a view to his repatriation to [LOCATION], which was discussed on [DATE_TIME] but did not come about.

On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court, acting under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code, extended Mr [PERSON]’s detention, as a psychiatric report produced at the request of that court stated that he was a dangerous person. The court took its decision under Article 25 (3) of the Criminal Code, after an official of the psychiatric hospital had stated to the court that the [DATE_TIME] review of the lawfulness of the detention should have taken place on [DATE_TIME] at the latest (see paragraph 20 above).

On [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] and a date in [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested his release, pointing out that the period for carrying out the [DATE_TIME] review had expired on [DATE_TIME]. On receiving the first of these applications, the court consulted a psychiatrist, who submitted a report on [DATE_TIME] recommending the applicant’s release subject to supervision (see paragraph 33 below). An application to exercise its supervisory jurisdiction (Dienstaufsichtsbeschwerde) was made to the Court of Appeal, which ordered the Regional Court to reach a decision speedily; on [DATE_TIME] the latter court ordered a further extension of the detention in issue. Taking into account the opinions of the psychiatric expert and the director of the hospital, filed on [DATE_TIME], it considered that there had been no fundamental change in Mr [PERSON]’s mental state. He was still suffering from paranoia [NRP], and if released would undoubtedly refuse to follow the necessary course of treatment; he would consequently be likely to bring numerous complaints or even carry out the threats he had made, in particular those against the prison staff (see paragraph 33 below). On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal and confirmed that the requirements for his release under Article 47 (2) of the Criminal Code were not satisfied.

Mr [PERSON] made further applications for release on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]. He was conditionally released on [DATE_TIME] in accordance with the court’s decision of [DATE_TIME], itself based on a psychiatric report dated [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 34 below). The court found that the applicant’s paranoia had admittedly worsened, but that it was primarily due to his detention (Haftquerulanz); the vexatious complaints and petitions (Rechtsquerulanz) did not constitute a danger within the meaning of Article 21 of the Criminal Code; since being detained the applicant had behaved with genuine aggressiveness on a few occasions only; although the possibility could not be excluded of his becoming aggressive in the event of frustration, his psychiatric history did not permit the conclusion that his abnormal personality would induce him to commit criminal offences; moreover, continued psychiatric treatment or treatment by drugs was not considered necessary by the expert, although it was recommended.

B. The medical treatment

On being returned to prison after his stay in the [LOCATION] psychiatric hospital from [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 16 above), Mr [PERSON] had begun a hunger strike on [DATE_TIME] as a protest against his detention and the refusal to give him his files. He collapsed on [DATE_TIME] and was transferred to a clinic where he received intensive medical care. On [DATE_TIME] he was transferred back to the [LOCATION] psychiatric hospital, where he remained until his release on [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 23 above).

As the applicant was in an extremely weak state when returned there, the director of the hospital ordered him to be force fed, pursuant to section 8 (3) of the Hospitals Law (see paragraph 51 below). The applicant refused all contact and refused to have any medical examination or treatment, and was also given sedatives against his will (three doses of 30mg each of Taractan IM); on [DATE_TIME] he was attached to a security bed, the net and straps of which he succeeded in cutting through. On [DATE_TIME] he was given a different neuroleptic (Sordinol IM), as infiltrations had appeared. He stopped refusing food on [DATE_TIME], after being allocated a single room and being given some of his files.

Mr [PERSON] again went on hunger strike from [DATE_TIME], on which date he allegedly eventually agreed to be fed through a tube (Sondenernährung) once [DATE_TIME]. However, he later denied that his consent had been validly given.

In view of the deterioration of his physical and mental state, he was injected by force with 90mg of [LOCATION] on [DATE_TIME], in order to bring about a state of somnolence ([LOCATION]) in which it would be possible to treat him by means of perfusions. Since he had resisted this with violence, the emergency team had had to overpower him. On [DATE_TIME] he was transferred to the intensive care unit, as he showed symptoms of pneumonia and nephritis; he stayed there until [DATE_TIME].

He had not made a complete recovery when he left, and he still needed treatment with antibiotics and neuroleptics. On his return to the closed unit he was handcuffed and a belt placed around his ankles because of the danger of aggression and the death threats he was making; the restraints were not removed until [DATE_TIME]. According to the Government, their position was changed regularly, in order to avoid nervous paralysis, and on [DATE_TIME] he had agreed to be fed by a woman doctor. The applicant stated, however, that other belts had been put around his thighs and stomach and had been untied for the first time only on [DATE_TIME]; in order to obtain his files and writing materials with which to write his complaints, he had continued his hunger strike without interruption, and had been artificially fed throughout this period.

From [DATE_TIME] the applicant calmed down and behaved in a more co-operative manner. Although he continued to insult the staff from time to time, he agreed to communicate with those around him and consented to being fed through a tube by a female doctor twice [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] he was given paper and a ballpoint pen.

Following a dispute about his correspondence, Mr [PERSON] was forbidden on [DATE_TIME] to watch television. As his physical resistance to the forced administration of neuroleptics had frequently been in vain and had even led to injuries (loss of teeth, broken ribs and bruises), he brought a complaint of assault on each occasion that he was given medicaments. These letters, which he claimed had not been communicated to the relevant authorities, filled six binders; they were given to him on his discharge.

During this period he continued to refuse, at least in part, to take nourishment other than through a tube, but on [DATE_TIME] he stated that he no longer needed to be fed artificially, as a doctor had persuaded him to end his hunger strike by explaining to him that it was endangering his life. Hospital reports had, however, stated that he appeared to be adequately nourished.

In an opinion of [DATE_TIME] an expert considered that conditional release of the applicant would be possible if certain accompanying psychiatric and social measures were taken. In his view, Mr [PERSON]’s behaviour was much improved, so that there was now virtually no danger.

After a further series of complaints which were regarded as vexatious, the Regional Court consulted the hospital on [DATE_TIME] as to the applicant’s possible release. On [DATE_TIME] an expert noted the progress which the applicant had made and expressed the opinion that troublesome behaviour did not constitute a risk within the meaning of Article 21 of the Criminal Code. However, in a letter of [DATE_TIME], the director of the hospital advised the court not to terminate Mr [PERSON]’s detention; as the treatment carried out, based on medication, had only a sedative effect, the possibility could not be excluded that if he were released, he would again become aggressive and dangerous. The Regional Court thereupon on [DATE_TIME] refused to release the applicant (see paragraph 22 above).

He eventually recovered his liberty on [DATE_TIME], after a further expert report dated [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 23 above).

C. The control of correspondence

While in detention Mr [PERSON] addressed an extremely large number of petitions and complaints to various authorities, relating inter alia to his medical treatment and the proceedings brought by him. As he considered that he did not have the necessary money, he refused on several occasions to put stamps on his letters, or sent them to the Ministry of Justice for that purpose. In order to stem this flow of correspondence, he was deprived from time to time of writing materials, and his unstamped letters were frequently returned to him, with the exception of those addressed to the public authorities, in particular the courts.

With respect to the letters written at the psychiatric hospital, the hospital management had agreed with the applicant’s curator that they would be transmitted to him regularly and it would be for him to decide whether it was necessary to send them on; this system would apply to all letters other than those to his lawyer, his adviser and the guardianship court. Mr [PERSON] has complained that even those letters were not all sent on.

When he left the hospital the applicant was given six binders containing the originals of these letters and also about fifty sealed letters; the postal register showed that the latter had never been sent to their addressees, namely the police, the public prosecutor’s office and the courts.

D. The restrictions on access to information

Mr [PERSON] also claimed that he had been deprived of reading matter, radio and television for long periods during his detention, in particular from [DATE_TIME] to [DATE_TIME] and from [DATE_TIME]; from [DATE_TIME] there had been no television set in his cell or in the ward. He alleged that these measures had been taken for disciplinary purposes only.

According to the Government, these measures were based on section 51 (1) of the Hospitals Law (see paragraph 51 below), had been justified for therapeutic reasons, and had lasted for a short time only on each occasion.

The Court decided to communicate the application to the Austrian Government and to grant priority to the application under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. It further requested the Hungarian Government to provide information regarding the status of the applicant’s asylum proceedings, as well as the reception conditions for unaccompanied minor asylum-seekers in [ LOCATION]. The applicant claims he was forced to lodge an asylum request and placed in an open camp. Allegedly, the [NRP] authorities did not give any consideration to the fact that he was a minor. The Traiskirchen Federal Asylum Office (Bundes­asylamt – hereinafter ‘the Asylum Office’) rejected the applicant’s asylum request in accordance with Article 16 § 1 (c) of Council Regulation (EC) No. 343/2003 (“the asylum office”) The applicant stated that his family had sent him away so he could live a safer life. His father had died in [LOCATION] in [DATE_TIME]. Asylgerichtshof quashed that decision pursuant to Article 66 § 2 of the Code of General Administrative Procedure (Allgemeines Verwaltungsverfahrensgesetz) It stated that the Asylum Office had failed to update its country information regarding the risk of refoulement of asylum‑seekers. The decision had not established the legal framework under which minors could be detained in [LOCATION] and what the conditions of detention were. The asylum request after his or her return under the [ Location] regulation was considered a subsequent asylum request. It was further established that appeals against asylum decisions at first instance and during the first proceedings had automatic suspensive effect. Asylum Court awarded suspensive effect to the applicant’s appeal against that decision, but on [DATE_TIME] dismissed it as unfounded. It pointed out that the [NRP] authorities had informed the Asylum Office that they had planned an age assessment, but could not carry it out because the applicant had left the country. The Asylum Office concluded that it hence did not consider itself legally obliged to make use of the sovereignty clause and rejected the asylum request. But the Asylum Court took note of a letter from the UNHCR Office in [LOCATION] dated [Date_TIME], seemingly citing problems with the techniques of age assessment. The Court ruled that the child would be returned to the UK. The child had been placed in the care of the carer of the child’s parents. The carer could not return the child to the caretakers until the child had reached the age of 16. The court ruled that this was not possible. The case has been adjourned until after the child reaches 16 years of age. The mother can apply to have the boy returned to her home in Scotland. Hungarian Parliament has adopted a comprehensive package of legislative amendments. The amendments’ reported aim is to ensure that asylum- seekers whose claims had not yet been decided might remain in [ LOCATION] pending an examination of the merits of their claims, and would not be subject to detention. The UNHCR appreciated the State’s reported intention to introduce additional legal guarantees concerning detention to ensure unhindered access to basic facilities such as toilets. The UNHCR noted that the number of asylum‑seekers detained had significantly declined in [DATE_TIME]. Asylum-seekers who applied for asylum immediately upon their arrival, or at the latest during their first interview with the immigration police, were no longer detained. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee raised concerns that there might be a threat that asylum-seekers were placed in alien policing detention upon return to [LOCATION] under the Dublin II Regulation. The proposed detention regime would also foresee the detention of first-time asylum- seekers as well as those whose cases had started even before the adoption of the proposed regulations. [PERSON] could not be excluded, as detention was up to the discretion of the Office of Immigration and Nationality. Hungarian Helsinki Committee noted that following the changes in legislation in [DATE_TIME] returnees were now considered as first-time applicants if they did not have a negative decision on the merits in their asylum procedure before leaving [LOCATION]. They had the chance to substantiate the reasons for their application in a detailed “in-merit procedure” and were not detained. Hungarian Helsinki Committee concluded that the amendments introducing a separate detention regime for asylum-seekers seriously weakened the judicial review of immigration and asylum detention and the right to appeal in asylum proceedings, and failed to ensure adequate reception conditions. In this note, the Hungarian Helsinki. Committee concludes that the. amendments introduced a separate Detention regime for Asylum-Seek seriously weakened. the judicial. review of Immigration and Asylum detention and. the right. to appeal. Hungarian Helsinki Committee calculated that on average, approximately 26% of all asylum-seekers were in asylum detention. Vulnerable people were not excluded from detention, with the exception of unaccompanied children. Alternatives to detention were available in the form of bail, a designated place to stay, and periodic reporting obligations. The scope of application of bail as alternative to asylum detention was not defined clearly enough, which it feared could result in the non-application of this measure in practice. The detention conditions for families were not appropriate. The majority of the social workers hardly spoke any foreign languages and were mainly performing administrative tasks rather than engaging with the detainees. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention visited [DATE_TIME] and [JANUARY_TIME]. In both countries there was an increase in the number of asylum-seekers. The report found there were no problems with the detention facilities. However, there were problems with access to medical care and other facilities.
